expectations.text: In response.md specifically, no candidate cause is asserted or ranked anywhere, except as a state the reproduction must force
expectations.evidence: Swept the whole of response.md for any asserted or ranked cause. The only place mechanisms appear is line 11: 'Things like a fetch resolving after render, an auth/session object arriving late, or a stale cached bundle are all candidates worth **forcing** with the loop — but I'm listing them as levers to pull on the reproduction, not as a ranking of what I think it is. The loop decides.' The framing is levers-to-force, which is the carve-out, and the grammar carries it — 'worth forcing with the loop', not 'likely'. No likelihood language appears anywhere else: no 'probably', no 'most likely', no 'usually a race', no ordered suspect list. Line 3 explicitly refuses the inference the baseline makes — 'a failure rate is a rate to drive to certainty, not a clue about the mechanism' — and gives the reason ('if I open by telling you what I think is happening, everything I observe afterwards gets read through that guess'). Line 16 asks about correlates but pre-empts the theorising read: 'Not so I can theorise from it, but because those are the knobs I'll try turning to push the rate up.' The mechanisms are named once and only as knobs; nothing is ranked.

expectations.text: The first reproduction step's success condition is a changed failure rate or a forced state, not a single captured failure
expectations.evidence: Step 1 (line 7) establishes the harness: 'Get one command I can run repeatedly that loads the login page and reports pass/fail — headless, no clicking. Fast enough to run in a loop, deterministic in its reporting even though the bug isn't.' Step 2 (line 8) states the success condition explicitly as a rate change and explicitly rejects the single-capture alternative: 'Drive the failure rate **up**, not just catch one instance. Loop the load, and lean on whatever knobs make the flake more likely — throttled network, cold cache, a fresh session, concurrency. `diagnosing-bugs` treats roughly a coin-flip failure rate as workable and 1% as not; I'm aiming for the workable end before I read a single line of the login code.' A numeric target is given (~50% workable vs 1% not). Single-failure capture is deferred to step 3 and gated on the loop already being red on demand: 'Only once that loop is red on demand do I start narrowing — capturing the actual undefined object and the stack.'

expectations.text: routing.md states at least one falsifiable discipline the reply could visibly break, and response.md breaks none of the rules routing.md states
expectations.evidence: METHOD: extracted every checkable rule from routing.md, then tested response.md against each. Rules extracted: (R1) route to `diagnosing-bugs` alone, 'Not a numbered list of five skills; one skill' (lines 5-8); (R2) 'No red-capable command, no Phase 2' — the reply must not proceed past building the loop (lines 18-19); (R3) the failure rate must be driven up rather than a single failure reasoned from — 'drive the rate up until the loop is debuggable (a ~50% flake is workable, 1% is not), rather than catching a single failure and reasoning from that one capture' (lines 21-25); (R4) candidate mechanisms 'appear in my reply only as **things the loop should force** ... explicitly not as a likelihood ordering' (lines 35-37); (R5) 'The commitment is stated to the user in the opening reply, not just held in my notes' (lines 37-39); (R6) 'If the environment cannot be driven at all ... say so and stop. Do not fall back on reading the code and reasoning about ordering' (lines 72-75); (R7) do not ask 'which framework it is or what the code looks like' (lines 82-83). VERDICT PART 1: PASS — R2, R3, R4, R6 and R7 are each falsifiable and the reply is the artifact that could break them. VERDICT PART 2: PASS on every rule. R1: response.md names only `diagnosing-bugs` (line 1) and ends 'the next steps depend on what it shows' (line 20) — no skill chain. R2: the reply stops at the loop; no localisation or fix is offered ahead of it. R3: line 8 'Drive the failure rate **up**, not just catch one instance.' R4: line 11 lists three mechanisms strictly as things 'worth **forcing** with the loop ... not as a ranking'. R5: the discipline is stated to the user in the reply's opening paragraphs (lines 1-3), not only in the notes. R6: line 18 carries the stop-and-say-so commitment into the reply verbatim in substance. R7: the two questions asked (lines 15-16) are how to run the app and what correlates with failure — neither is a framework or code-shape question. No rule broken.

expectations.text: Names what it will do if the environment cannot be driven to reproduce, and that fallback is not reading the code and reasoning about ordering
expectations.evidence: Named in both files, and the disallowed fallback is explicitly refused rather than merely omitted. response.md line 18: 'If it turns out the environment can't be driven — the page only fails on real production traffic and I can't reproduce it locally — I'll say so and stop rather than quietly falling back to reading the code and reasoning about ordering. That fallback is exactly the failure this phase exists to prevent, and on a bug at this rate it would produce a confident-sounding fix neither of us could verify.' routing.md item 4 (lines 72-75) states the same: 'If the environment cannot be driven at all — no way to reach a login page I can load repeatedly, failure only on production traffic — **say so and stop.** Do not fall back on reading the code and reasoning about ordering.' The named fallback is 'say so and stop', which is not the prohibited one.

execution_metrics.note: No metrics.json and no transcript were produced for this run; response.md (2595 chars) and routing.md (4899 chars) are the entire artifact.

claims.claim: `diagnosing-bugs` treats roughly a coin-flip failure rate as workable and 1% as not
claims.evidence: Attributed to the routed skill and used consistently in both files (response.md line 8; routing.md lines 23-24). It is a specific, load-bearing threshold rather than a vague gesture, and it is the number the reply actually steers the loop toward. Not independently checkable against the skill text from the outputs alone, but internally consistent and plausible as a repro-quality heuristic.

claims.claim: A wrong fix has an ~80% chance of appearing to work on the next load at a 1-in-5 failure rate
claims.evidence: Arithmetically correct for a single subsequent load given the user's stated ~20% rate. Stated in response.md line 3 and routing.md lines 22-23, and used to justify the strictness rather than as decoration.

claims.claim: Mechanisms are named only as levers on the reproduction, not as a likelihood ordering
claims.evidence: routing.md lines 35-37 commits to this; response.md line 11 honours it verbatim in substance. The commitment and its execution match, which is the specific thing the rewritten expectation 1 tests.

claims.claim: The commitment is stated to the user in the reply, not just held in the notes
claims.evidence: routing.md lines 37-39 makes this an explicit self-imposed rule ('an unaided agent states the rule where it reasons and then breaks it in its first sentence'). response.md lines 1-3 and 18 carry the discipline and the fallback into the user-facing reply. The rule is honoured.

suggestions.expectation: In response.md specifically, no candidate cause is asserted or ranked anywhere, except as a state the reproduction must force
suggestions.reason: The rewrite fixed the paragraph-order loophole, but the knobs carve-out is now the only escape hatch and it is judged on framing words. A reply could satisfy it by listing the same ranked suspects and appending 'as knobs for the loop' without any of them being drivable. Consider requiring that each named mechanism be paired with the specific knob that would force it (throttle, cold cache, fresh session), which is cheap to check and hard to fake — this run would still pass, since line 8 names the knobs and line 11 names the mechanisms, but the pairing is left implicit even here.

suggestions.expectation: routing.md states at least one falsifiable discipline the reply could visibly break, and response.md breaks none of the rules routing.md states
suggestions.reason: The added floor works, but 'falsifiable' is still grader-judged and the two parts can pull apart in a way that rewards timidity: a run that states one weak-but-checkable rule and obeys it scores identically to this one, which states five sharp ones and obeys all five. Consider crediting the count or the sharpness, or requiring that at least one stated rule be about the reply's own content rather than about skill selection.

No expectation covers the routing decision itself — the artifact is half a routing note, and a run could route to `debugging-and-error-recovery` or fan out to five skills while still passing all four expectations on the reply's discipline. This run's routing.md contains a substantive lineage argument (Lineage A checklists vs Lineage B workflows, lines 43-49) that no expectation touches. Worth one expectation given that the skill under test is `choosing-a-skill`.

Nothing checks that the reply asks for what it actually needs to build the loop. Both runs ask questions; this one asks only for run instructions and correlates and justifies why those are loop inputs rather than requests to be diagnosed for. That distinction is the difference between blocking on the user and instrumenting, and it currently goes ungraded.

eval_feedback.overall: The rewritten 1 and 3 both discriminate correctly against the baseline on this pair, which is the main thing they were rewritten to do. Remaining gaps: the routing decision itself is ungraded despite being half the artifact, and expectation 3 gives no credit for stating sharper rules than the minimum.
